pages.title: The supplied Midterm 1 exam format
pages.c: **The supplied Midterm 1 review describes ten short essay questions, with about 100–250 words expected for each answer.** Each question contains three or four gradeable items, so an answer can earn partial credit by explaining the relevant parts accurately.
support: The review describes that exam as open book and says that memorizing names and dates is unnecessary. Preparation should emphasize explaining concepts, using the relevant examples and connecting experimental findings to the claims they support.
pages.d: Practice answering a focused question in a connected paragraph or two. Identify the distinctions the question asks about and explain each one with the appropriate evidence. The ten-question, open-book format belongs to the supplied Midterm 1 review.

pages.title: Experience changes activation dynamics
pages.c: **Word activation develops over time, and experience can change how quickly a word becomes available.** A frequently encountered word might begin with a higher baseline of activation, receive stronger input through its incoming connections, or reach a recognition criterion more readily because its threshold has changed. These are different ways for a model to explain a frequency effect.
support: A higher baseline gives the word a head start before the current input arrives. Stronger incoming connections make a given input produce a larger activation change. A lower recognition threshold reduces the activation required for a response. Each mechanism links prior experience to faster identification without treating frequency as a separate label that simply causes speed.

The activation curve for CAVE rises as the input is processed and then falls. Other word representations remain much less active. The curves describe changing states within a model, rather than measured firing rates from individual neurons. Different computational models can implement the effect of experience in different ways.
pages.d: A frequency effect asks why words encountered often are usually identified more quickly. An activation account can answer by specifying what experience changes in the system. It may change the starting level of a word’s activity, the effectiveness of its connections, or the criterion for deciding that the word has been recognized. Those alternatives make the explanation more precise than saying that familiar words are easier.
pages.visual: Time runs along the horizontal axis and activation along the vertical axis. CAVE has a prominent peak above the smaller curves for other word representations. The graph illustrates activation unfolding after input. It does not separately plot high-frequency and low-frequency conditions, so the baseline, connection and threshold proposals explain possible frequency mechanisms rather than three measured effects in this figure.

pages.title: Mediated priming depends on the response task
pages.c: **Balota and Lorch tested whether activation can travel through an unpresented connecting concept.** LION and STRIPES are linked through TIGER, even though LION and STRIPES are not directly associated. The prime–target comparisons included directly related pairs, mediated pairs, a neutral prime and an unrelated prime.
support: In lexical decision, participants judged whether the target was a word. Directly related primes facilitated responses, but mediated primes did not improve performance relative to the neutral or unrelated conditions.

In pronunciation, participants read the target aloud. Both directly related and mediated primes facilitated responses. The mediated benefit supports activation spreading beyond a directly associated concept. The contrast between tasks also matters. Balota and Lorch proposed that characteristics of lexical decision masked the mediated effect, so the absence of that effect in one response task was not evidence that activation could never reach the indirectly connected target.
pages.d: A mediated prime reaches a target through another concept. LION can activate TIGER, which connects to STRIPES. Balota and Lorch compared this indirect relationship with direct relatedness and with control primes. Direct priming appeared in both lexical decision and pronunciation, while mediated priming appeared in pronunciation. The response task therefore changed whether the indirect influence was detectable.
pages.visual: The article title contrasts pronunciation with lexical decision, and its abstract identifies LION–STRIPES as the mediated pair with TIGER as the connecting concept. LION–TIGER and TIGER–STRIPES illustrate the direct relationships that make the indirect route possible.

pages.title: Activation can reach an indirectly connected word
pages.c: **Mediated priming occurs when a prime helps a target through an intervening association.** LION is connected to TIGER, and TIGER is connected to STRIPES. Activating LION can therefore increase activity at STRIPES even though the two are not directly associated. TIGER supplies the connecting route without having to be presented as an extra stimulus.
support: A direct association links a prime to its target in one step. The mediated relationship requires activity to pass through the network. Facilitation between indirectly related words is informative because the model must explain how activity reaches a word that the prime does not directly activate.

The connected LION, TIGER and STRIPES nodes express the same indirect relationship when the illustrated input is STRIPES. The example of LION priming STRIPES and the pictured STRIPES input describe the network from opposite ends. Both depend on TIGER as the intervening node.
pages.d: The important relation is the route through TIGER. LION and STRIPES do not share a direct association in this example, but each is associated with TIGER. A spreading-activation account predicts that activity can influence the farther node through that shared connection. This is why an indirect priming benefit provides evidence about the organization of the network.
pages.visual: STRIPES is the input label beneath the three lexical nodes, and the emphasized nodes and connecting lines represent activity spreading through the network. Follow the indirect path through TIGER when relating the picture to the LION–STRIPES example.

pages.title: Reading the mediated-priming response times
pages.c: **Pronunciation was faster after a mediated prime than after either control prime.** Averaged across the two timing conditions, the mean latency was 549 ms for directly related primes, 558 ms for mediated primes, 577 ms for neutral primes and 575 ms for unrelated primes. The mediated advantage was 19 ms relative to neutral and 17 ms relative to unrelated primes.
support: Stimulus onset asynchrony, or SOA, is the time between the onset of the prime and the onset of the target. The experiment used 250 ms and 500 ms SOAs. At 250 ms, the mediated condition averaged 558 ms compared with 570 ms for neutral and 574 ms for unrelated primes. At 500 ms, the mediated mean was again 558 ms compared with 583 ms and 576 ms for the two controls.

Lower pronunciation latency means that the participant began saying the target sooner. The direct condition was fastest, but the indirect relationship also helped. These small response-time differences are useful because carefully chosen control conditions identify an influence that would be difficult to notice in everyday speech.
pages.d: The central comparison is mediated versus control priming. At both SOAs, a mediated prime reduced the time required to start pronouncing the target. The overall mediated mean of 558 ms falls between direct priming at 549 ms and the neutral and unrelated controls at 577 ms and 575 ms. The pattern connects the indirect relation between words to a measurable benefit in pronunciation.
pages.visual: Rows distinguish 250 ms SOA, 500 ms SOA and the mean across SOAs. Columns distinguish related, mediated, neutral and unrelated primes. The table reports pronunciation latencies in milliseconds, so compare smaller values with larger values within a row. SOA describes the experimental timing, while the values inside the four condition columns describe response latency.

questions.stem: What makes a minimal pair evidence that two sounds represent different phonemes?
choices: Replacing one sound with the other changes the word’s meaning while the surrounding sounds remain the same.
The two sounds are produced at different places in the mouth, regardless of word meaning.
The sounds use different letters in ordinary spelling.
Both sounds can occur somewhere in the same language, even in unrelated words.
questions.why: A minimal pair isolates the sound difference and demonstrates that the difference is contrastive. Articulatory or spelling differences alone do not establish a phonemic contrast.

questions.stem: Why is the plural in “two forks” a useful example of inflection?
choices: The sentence context requires a plural form, and the noun keeps its lexical identity.
Adding the plural creates a new lexical concept unrelated to FORK.
Every plural must be formed by adding the same spoken suffix.
Plurality is chosen independently of the rest of the sentence.
questions.why: Inflection expresses a grammatical distinction required by the sentence. Its function is predictable even when the form is irregular, as in two mice.

questions.stem: Which proposal explains a word-frequency effect within an activation model?
choices: Repeated experience strengthens incoming connections, so a given input activates the word more quickly.
Frequent words are recognized before any sensory input is processed because they have no threshold.
Frequent words necessarily contain fewer phonemes, so lexical activation is irrelevant.
Experience changes a word’s meaning each time while leaving its activation dynamics unchanged.
questions.why: Changes in baseline, connection strength or recognition threshold can link experience to recognition speed. The explanation must identify how processing changes.

questions.stem: Which pattern did Balota and Lorch report for mediated priming?
choices: Mediated facilitation appeared in pronunciation but not in lexical decision.
Mediated facilitation appeared in lexical decision but not in pronunciation.
Only mediated primes facilitated pronunciation, while directly related primes did not.
Both tasks showed identical mediated effects and no direct priming.
questions.why: Direct priming appeared in both tasks. The mediated benefit in pronunciation supports spreading activation beyond directly associated concepts, while the lexical-decision result shows that response-task characteristics affect its detection.

questions.stem: What was the point of Jackson’s criticism of a simple localization account?
choices: Locating damage that destroys speech does not by itself locate the entire speech function.
A lesion can never provide useful evidence about language.
Tan’s difficulty proved that his hearing was absent.
Every word must be stored in a separate cortical center.
questions.why: A damaged area may be important for a process without containing the whole process. Jackson’s criticism challenges the inference from the location of a disabling lesion to the complete location of speech.

questions.stem: Why does “Where’d I bring it when I put it in” support distinguishing a lemma from its inflected form?
choices: BRING appears as the base form bring after did, although the intended sentence used brought in the other position.
The speaker moved the fully inflected form brought into the question without changing it.
The error replaced a verb with a noun that had no grammatical role.
The error removed both verbs and preserved only the tense endings.
questions.why: The intended sentence was “Where’d I put it when I brought it in.” The exchanged lexical choice is fitted to the grammatical requirements of its new position. After did, BRING is expressed as bring.

questions.stem: What does “a language needer learns” preserve from the intended “a language learner needs”?
choices: The grammatical frame and the affix positions, even though the lexical roots exchange.
The original word order of the fully formed words learner and needs.
Only the meanings of the words, with no preserved syntactic structure.
A past-tense ending attached to each verb.
questions.why: NEED enters the position with derivational -er, while LEARN enters the verb position with third-person singular -s. The stranded affixes distinguish lexical selection from the frame into which the lexical items are placed.

questions.stem: Why did matching high-frequency and low-frequency words for length matter?
choices: It tested whether the observed frequency effect could be explained by the usual difference in word length.
It made the words equally frequent, removing the independent variable.
It ensured that every picture named the same object.
It proved that no other stimulus property could ever affect naming.
questions.why: High-frequency words are generally shorter. A frequency effect that survives length matching cannot be reduced to that particular length difference.

questions.stem: Which result helped place semantic blocking at lemma selection in the Belke study?
choices: Homogeneous sets increased gaze duration after the first cycle, without a corresponding blocking effect in gaze-to-speech lag.
Homogeneous sets increased speech duration and shortened gaze duration by the same amount.
Blocking occurred only in gaze-to-speech lag, while naming and gaze duration were identical.
Every measure showed the same blocking effect starting on the first cycle.
questions.why: The difference in gaze duration, together with the absence of a corresponding lag effect, supports the proposed distinction between selection and later phonological encoding. Speech duration also showed no blocking effect.

questions.stem: Why was introducing new items in cycle 5 informative about semantic blocking?
choices: Blocking persisted for the new category members even though the benefit from repeating those exact items was lost.
The new items removed every difference between homogeneous and heterogeneous sets.
The new items had already been named in cycles 1–4, so they isolated motor repetition.
The manipulation tested only whether participants remembered the cycle numbers.
questions.why: Both conditions slowed when new items appeared, but the homogeneous disadvantage remained. The blocking effect therefore generalized beyond the exact lexical items repeatedly named before cycle 5.

written.prompt: Explain how “Where’d I put it when I brought it in” becoming “Where’d I bring it when I put it in” distinguishes functional and positional processing. Use about 100–250 words.
answer: At the functional level, the speaker selects the lemmas PUT and BRING and assigns their semantic roles. The error exchanges these lexical choices.

At the positional level, the sentence has a grammatical frame with a question containing did and an embedded past-tense clause. The verb after did must take the base form, while the embedded verb occupies a past-tense position.

BRING is therefore realized as bring in the first position rather than as the originally intended brought. This adjustment is evidence that a lemma can be selected separately from the final inflected form.
The error preserves much of the sentence’s structure while changing which lexical item fills each verb position. A model that only moved fully formed words would miss the grammatical adjustment.

written.prompt: Explain why Belke and colleagues interpreted cyclic semantic blocking as an effect involving lexical selection. Connect the naming result, the eye-movement measures and the introduction of new items. Use about 100–250 words.
answer: Participants repeatedly named objects from homogeneous semantic sets or heterogeneous sets. Related sets produced slower naming after the first cycle, so semantic relatedness created interference rather than a simple naming benefit.
In the selection model, category-related words activate one another. A target can become more active while selection becomes harder because competing lemmas are also active.

Homogeneous sets increased gaze duration, while gaze-to-speech lag and speech duration did not show the corresponding blocking effect. This pattern supports placing the interference at lemma selection rather than simply at phonological encoding or speech execution.

When new items appeared in cycle 5, both conditions slowed as item-specific repetition benefits were lost. Blocking nevertheless generalized to those new items, which argues against explaining the effect solely as repetition of the same item list.

Matched or normed visual stimuli and a visual-recognition control addressed recognition differences. The words were phonologically dissimilar, and the gaze-versus-lag comparison further addressed a phonological explanation.
